frameworks.name: Evolutionary Heuristics vs. Economic Rationality
frameworks.definition: Human behavioral heuristics evolved as near-optimal solutions under imperfect information and imperfect trust; labeling them biases misunderstands their adaptive purpose.

frameworks.name: Satisficing Framework (Herbert Simon)
frameworks.definition: In real-world decisions with no mathematical optimum, the best attainable outcome is one that is good enough (satisficing), not theoretically perfect (optimizing).

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that behavioral science and behavioral economics should only be studied alongside evolutionary psychology and evolutionary theory, because without that pairing, practitioners will incorrectly interpret evolved heuristics as irrational biases rather than as near-optimal solutions adapted to imperfect real-world conditions.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: practitioners studying heuristics and biases in behavioral economics or behavioral science
claims.mechanism: The word bias carries a pejorative connotation that primes analysts to accept the economic view that deviations from the standard economic model are sub-optimal, when in fact many deviations are optimal adaptations to conditions of imperfect information and imperfect trust.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the foundational assumptions of standard economic theory — that humans are individual utility-maximizing actors operating in standalone transactions under conditions of perfect information and perfect trust — are not reasonable simplifications but fundamental distortions of reality, because conditions of perfect information and perfect trust exist in practice somewhere between very rarely and never.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Economic assumptions of perfect information and perfect trust are empirically false; human brains have not evolved to operate under those conditions and were instead selected to make good non-catastrophic decisions under imperfect information and imperfect trust.
bounded_by: Even if perfect information and perfect trust could theoretically be created, human cognition has not evolved to operate under those conditions, so the distortion would persist regardless

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that human brains evolved specifically to make non-catastrophic decisions under imperfect, asymmetric information and imperfect trust — not to optimize expected utility — because any ancestor who was not good at solving those problems under realistic conditions would have left few descendants.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Evolutionary selection pressure filtered out individuals unable to make adequate decisions under imperfect information and imperfect trust; the surviving population is therefore systematically adapted for satisficing under realistic conditions rather than optimizing under ideal ones.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that many evolved heuristics are not cognitively inferior substitutes for mathematical optimization; they are the best achievable solution given the actual information available, and calling them biases is a dangerous misuse of language because it frames clever adaptations as stupidity.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: when the information required for mathematical optimization is unavailable or untrustworthy
claims.mechanism: Mathematical optimization requires complete and trusted input data; when such data is unavailable (as in most real-world decisions), a heuristic that leverages available signals is functionally superior to an optimization formula that would yield garbage output from garbage inputs.
bounded_by: Heuristics can be inferior to mathematical optimization when complete, trusted information is genuinely available

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues, citing Herbert Simon, that in most real-world decisions there is no mathematical formula for finding an optimal solution, so satisficing — finding a solution that is good enough given available information — is the best achievable outcome, not a cognitive failure.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: decisions without a closed-form mathematical optimum, such as choosing a spouse, buying a house, or making business strategy decisions
bounded_by: Does not apply to decisions with well-defined mathematical optima (e.g., inventory calculations with known demand distributions)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that heuristics have a survival advantage over mathematical reasoning because heuristics are likely heritable whereas mathematical skills must be taught; this makes reliable heuristics far more valuable from a population-level survival standpoint than skills that require active transmission across generations.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: population-level survival reliability over evolutionary time scales
claims.mechanism: Heritable cognitive shortcuts are transmitted automatically across generations without requiring education, whereas mathematical reasoning requires cultural infrastructure to transmit; heritable heuristics therefore survive generation gaps and social disruptions that would eliminate learned mathematical skills.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the standard economic model wrongly labels human behavior as irrational whenever it deviates from model predictions, when the correct diagnosis is that the model is built on false assumptions; the model is wrong, not the humans.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Economic theory constructs its rationality benchmark from assumptions that are false in practice (perfect information, perfect trust, utility maximization); deviations from a false benchmark are evidence of incorrectness in the benchmark, not irrationality in the observed behavior.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that a heuristic operating on incorruptible observable signals is strictly superior to mathematical optimization in adversarial environments where the party holding the relevant information has an incentive to deceive, because mathematical optimization on corrupted or missing inputs yields unreliable outputs.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: adversarial information environment: the counterparty possesses the key data and has an active incentive to withhold or distort it
real-time decision requiring immediate commitment with no opportunity to gather additional trusted information
claims.mechanism: A heuristic based on an incorruptible observable signal (e.g., angle of gaze to a moving ball) bypasses the deception problem entirely; mathematical optimization on the same signal set would require trusting inputs that the adversary controls.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the information source is both trusted and complete

examples.text: Rory Sutherland describes the ball-catching heuristic identified by Gerd Gigerenzen: a fielder catching a high-flying baseball does not compute the landing point from velocity, angle, and air resistance — information that is unavailable and, in the case of the batsman, actively withheld. Instead the fielder looks up at the ball, notes the angle of gaze, and moves at whatever speed and direction keeps that angle constant. The path is a slight curve rather than a straight line — a minor efficiency cost — but the heuristic works reliably without any trusted input data. Sutherland notes that dogs apply the same heuristic with frisbees, and argues that calling such a strategy a bias is a nonsense.

Rory Sutherland describes the Sullenberger Hudson River landing (2009) as an example of fast-and-frugal heuristic reasoning under extreme time pressure. After a bird strike knocked out both engines, Captain Sullenberger assessed in roughly five seconds whether he could reach Teterborough Airport. Rather than computing glide equations, he used the glider pilot heuristic: enter the shallowest possible glide, look forward, and identify which points on the visual field are moving upward (unreachable) versus downward (reachable). Teterborough appeared on the wrong side of that line, so Sullenberger immediately redirected to the Hudson River. Sutherland frames this as finding the best non-catastrophic option under uncertainty, not the mathematically optimal one, because no mathematically optimal option existed.

Rory Sutherland opens with a joke about a physicist, biologist, and mathematician whose faculty budgets are cut and who attempt to crack horse racing to recoup funding. The biologist makes little progress noting that heredity matters; the mathematician concludes the market cannot be beaten statistically; the physicist declares the problem solved — by assuming the horse is a perfect sphere racing in a vacuum. Sutherland uses this to illustrate that economic theory makes similarly unrealistic idealizing assumptions (perfect information, perfect trust, individual utility maximization) that make the model mathematically tractable but empirically false.

practices.text: Study behavioral science and behavioral economics only in parallel with evolutionary psychology and evolutionary theory, so that evolved heuristics are interpreted as adaptive solutions rather than dismissed as irrational biases.

When evaluating whether a human behavior is rational or irrational, first audit the assumptions of the benchmark model before concluding the behavior is defective; the benchmark itself may be the source of error.
In adversarial or informationally incomplete environments, prefer heuristics that operate on incorruptible observable signals over mathematical models that require trusted, complete inputs.
